module_title: Windows OS - File Systems (NTFS/FAT), Extensions, and Administrative Utilities
introduction: This intermediate tier moves past simple navigation into how Windows internally manages files and data storage. We explore file allocation table standards, data identification tags (extensions), and the built-in troubleshooting hubs used by power users.

core_concepts.title: File Systems: FAT32 vs. NTFS
core_concepts.description:
A file system dictates how data is indexed, stored, and retrieved from a hard drive.
- FAT32 (File Allocation Table): An older standard. It is highly compatible but has a fatal limitation—it cannot store a single file that is larger than 4GB. Mainly used on older USB flash drives.
- NTFS (New Technology File System): The modern default file system for Windows (XP through 11). It supports secure file permissions, automated encryption, data recovery, and has no practical file-size limits.

core_concepts.title: File Extensions
core_concepts.description:
The 3 or 4-letter suffix following the dot at the end of a filename. It tells Windows what type of data the file contains and which application should open it. 
Examples: `.txt` (Notepad), `.docx` (MS Word), `.exe` (Executable/Software Installer), `.jpg`/`.png` (Image files).

core_concepts.title: Control Panel & Settings
core_concepts.description: The centralized configuration hub of Windows. It allows users to safely install/uninstall software, manage user profile accounts, adjust accessibility, and configure connected hardware like printers.

core_concepts.title: The System Clipboard
core_concepts.description: A temporary, volatile memory cache allocated by Windows. When you copy (Ctrl+C) or cut (Ctrl+X) text or an image, that data is invisibly held inside the Clipboard until you execute a paste (Ctrl+V) command.

important_entities.name: Task Manager
important_entities.significance: Accessed via `Ctrl + Shift + Esc`. It displays real-time hardware consumption (CPU, RAM) and allows users to kill frozen or 'Not Responding' programs using the 'End Task' action.

important_entities.name: Recycle Bin
important_entities.significance: A temporary holding zone for deleted files. Files sent here can be 'Restored' back to their original location unless the bin is explicitly emptied.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Pressing the standard 'Delete' key simply moves a file to the Recycle Bin. To bypass the bin and permanently delete a file directly from the hard drive, the correct hotkey combination is `Shift + Delete`.
In acronym-based options, examiners often write 'File Access Table' for FAT. Ensure you pick 'File ALLOCATION Table'.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Whenever you see `.exe`, remember it stands for 'Executable'—meaning it is a program or installer that will run code automatically when clicked.

exam_strategy_tips: File extensions and core keyboard shortcuts (like `Shift + Delete` or `Ctrl + Shift + Esc`) are premium targets in standard tier-1 papers. Ensure you have the file type associations completely mapped out.
